newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Sigma sees good insurance growth in East Europe.
newsitem.headline: Sigma sees good insurance growth in East Europe.

text.p: Insurers have good prospects for growth in eastern and central Europe as economies there stabilise and expand and regulatory control improves, according to Swiss Re's research bulletin Sigma.
Mounting competition from foreign companies will also lead to considerable restructuring, especially at big former monopolies after privatisation, Sigma said in its latest edition.
"There are good prospects for growth in Eastern Europe's insurance industry," the report said.
"In the 1997-2002 period, we anticipate inflation-adjusted premium volume growth in Eastern Europe averaging 5-8 percent in non-life and 7-12 percent in life insurance," it wrote.
This compared to expected GDP growth around four to six percent in the same period, it said.
The study covered 10 countries -- Bulgaria, Croatia, the Czech Republic, Estonia, Hungary, Poland, Russia, Slovakia, Slovenia and Ukraine.
Premium volumes in these countries were $12 billion in 1995, the report said. The biggest markets were Russia, Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary with three quarters of total premiums.
The dominant lines of business were motor, property and fire insurance with agricultural insurance still important but on the decline.
"Life insurance accounts for only a low level of premium volume although this is quite typical for countries with such low income levels," Sigma said.
Sigma said it anticipated a lasting period of restructuring as new companies become increasily important, foreign companies make their presence felt and some firms disappear.
"The structural changes will, however, be taking place in an altogether favourable environment," Sigma said.
It said the regulatory environment was improving as most eastern European countries had adopted insurance legislation based on European Union law.
Supervision functioned well in most places but remained insufficient in Romania, Bulgaria, Russia and the Baltic states.
